title: scratchpad integration notes: rtx custom op benchmarks and allocator experiments
body:
Purpose:
Short scratchpad of integration experiments that I ran to compare three different ways of wiring kernels/allocators together for medium-size LLM inference (70B-ish open models). Focus is on practical tradeoffs: latency tail, memory fragmentation, KV-cache growth, and complexity of moving between Triton-hosted models, TensorRT plugins, and a small set of custom fused ops. This is intentionally informal — notes to help design the next prototype that implements hybrid routing + pooled allocator.

Hardware and baseline:
- GPU: NVIDIA A100 40GB (PCIe) and one RTX 6000 for small regression runs.
- Driver/CUDA: 525.x, cuDNN 8.x. TensorRT 8.6, Triton 2.14 (internal build), serving-runtime branch: scratch/allocator-experiments.
- Model: open-architecture 70B (sharded across GPUs for throughput experiments, single-shard for latency experiments). We used FP16 for Triton and TensorRT; INT8 calibration attempted for a subset of layers (not stable for generation quality).
- Baseline allocator: cudaMalloc/cudaFree on each request. Secondary: pooled allocator based on rmm/cnmem style pool (simple bump allocator with reuse).

Experiment matrix (summary):
- Kernel backends: Triton (separate model instance), TensorRT engine (serialized plugin): both using standard runtimes; Custom fused-ops (in-process) compiled as CUDA kernels and linked as a plugin layer in our runtime.
- Allocators: default (cudaMalloc), pooled (pre-allocated 80% of GPU mem minus system), pinned host staging, and hybrid (pinned host + small device pool).
- KV-cache policies: dynamic grow (append pages), fixed-slice prealloc, on-device shrink-to-fit.
- Workloads: single-stream interactive (batch=1) with varying seq lengths [32, 256, 1024, 2048], and multi-client burst (concurrent N=8, 16).

Key observations:
1) Cold-start latency for TensorRT engines hosted in Triton is dominated by the Triton RPC/IPC path (20–40ms extra p50) when the engine lives in a separate process. If Triton and the serving runtime are co-located in-process (embedding plugin into runtime), the application-level overhead drops ~18–22ms for batch=1.

2) Custom fused attention kernels (single process) provide the best p50/p95 for long contexts (>1024) because they avoid kernel-launch churn when we implement a single fused pass that handles KV cache read/write. Observed: ~15–22% p95 reduction vs TensorRT engine + standard attention layers for seq=2048 in single client runs.

3) Fragmentation matters: naive cudaMalloc/cudaFree every request leads to a noisy memory footprint under burst concurrency. Even with 40GB, fragmentation triggered OOMs during N=16 bursts for seq=1024. A pooled allocator (bump + free list) reduced OOM events to zero in our runs and improved p95 by ~12% (less GC stalls).

4) KV cache strategy tradeoffs:
   - Prealloc slices (fixed) are simplest: easy mapping, constant-time pointer arithmetic, low fragmentation. But wasteful for workloads that rarely reach long contexts.
   - Dynamic grow (append pages when needed) is memory efficient but increases p95 under burst due to intermittent allocations and page transitions.
   - Proposed middle ground: slice-on-first-growth — keep small preallocated per-request slice (enough for 256 tokens), then switch to page-append if growth required. This gives 90% of memory savings with 70% of the p95 tail benefit.

5) Cross-process vs in-process placement: Triton/TensorRT as a process boundary simplifies isolation and reuse (multiple tenants can reuse engine). But moving kv-cache between processes (IPC + pinned host staging) added 8–18ms for each large context restore. For many interactive apps that's unacceptable. In-process custom kernels allowed direct pointer sharing of KV pages (zero-copy) which recovered the latency. Risk: one tenant's leak/bug can impact the whole process.

Microbenchmarks (representative numbers, single A100, software stack above):
- Workload: batch=1, seq=256, 1 query generation (gen len 128)
   - Triton(TensorRT engine) in separate process: p50=120ms, p95=210ms, tokens/sec ~ 75
   - TensorRT in-process (engine loaded into runtime): p50=98ms, p95=185ms, tokens/sec ~ 92
   - Custom fused ops (in-process): p50=88ms, p95=152ms, tokens/sec ~ 105
- Workload: batch=1, seq=2048, gen 512
   - Triton separate: p50=480ms, p95=720ms, OOM events during bursts (N=8)
   - TensorRT in-process: p50=420ms, p95=610ms
   - Custom fused ops: p50=360ms, p95=510ms

- Memory overhead (observed resident GPU memory, approximate):
   - Triton separate process: model engine + Triton overhead ~ 6–8GB extra on top of model weights (IPC buffers, pinned host staging).
   - TensorRT in-process: engine memory ~ weights + working buffers (~3–5GB)
   - Custom fused ops: minimal transient buffers, but peaks if we choose naive dynamic KV pages. With pooled allocator and slice-on-first-growth, peak ~ weights + 2–3GB.

Design notes and implications for serving-runtime:
- Hybrid routing policy: send short-context/bursty requests to Triton-managed engines (fast reuse, easier multi-tenant). Route long-context or latency-sensitive requests to in-process custom kernels. This requires a fast decision layer (latency budget + estimated peak tokens) and ability to route sessions to the same backend for caching to be effective.

- Allocator API proposal (lightweight):
   - reserve(size_hint) -> opaque handle
   - commit(handle, usage_size) -> pointer on device (or failure)
   - release(handle)
   - snapshot_kv(handle) -> export descriptor for IPC (only for special allowed backends)
  Rationale: separate reserve from commit to support pooled bump behavior and fall back to cudaMalloc when pool exhausted. Snapshot allows safe cross-process handoff when running with Triton.

- KV cache lifecycle: keep per-session metadata tiny (session id, allocated slices list) and implement background compaction (coalescing small free slices every X minutes). Compaction frequency should be tunable by customer > default: 5 minutes.

- Fallback and safety: if in-process custom kernel crashes, we must have a fast fallback to a Triton instance (maybe slightly older model variant) to keep the service alive. To make this feasible, we must ensure model compatibility across variants and maintain an external state store for session->backend mapping.

Operational notes from runs:
- RMM-style pool needs to reserve enough to avoid eviction but not so much we starve other processes. On a shared host, reserve 70–80% of free GPU memory is reasonable; on dedicated we can be more aggressive.
- Calibrated INT8 in TensorRT showed token-quality regressions in ~1.2% of prompts in our QA set — avoid INT8 for generation by default. FP16 remains primary.
- Triton metrics are helpful but need extra tracing for per-request KV-copy times. Add a small hook to emit KV delta sizes and copy latency as tags.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Measure fragmentation under long-running process with thousands of short sessions. Does our compaction strategy keep fragmentation within bounds?
2) Can we implement a small persistent device-resident slab allocator for KV pages that survives over model reloads? (tradeoff: added complexity vs faster reuse).
3) Evaluate security footprint of in-process custom kernels: how does memory corruption or OOM in a single session impact other tenants? How to sandbox?
4) Explore a hybrid IPC: keep engines in Triton but allow direct GPU shared memory region for KV pages (mmap/pinned memory) to avoid copy. Is this feasible with existing Triton -> CUDA driver constraints?

Action items / TODOs:
- [Priya] build a small prototype of reserve/commit API and integrate into local serving-runtime branch (due end of week).
- [Miguel] run long-duration fragmentation test (72h) with 1000 short sessions and report memory curves.
- [Zoe] draft a canary rollback plan for in-process custom kernels (how to detect and cut over to Triton).
- [Daniel] prepare a short tech brief for product on tradeoffs and recommended default: pooled allocator with slice-on-first-growth, FP16 in-process engines for latency sensitive customers; Triton-managed engines for multi-tenant cost efficiency.

Notes to reviewers:
- These are rough numbers; environment variance matters. Please re-run critical benchmarks on your hardware configuration and paste results into this doc (copy/paste) rather than commenting numbers in-line.
- If you have a Triton configuration that supports shared device regions for KV pages, tag the link in linked_artifacts so we can iterate.

End of scratchpad.
